before.prompt: Combine: I bought three things. They were a notebook, two pens, and a folder. Which version uses the pause before the list correctly?
choices: I bought three things: a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
I bought three things a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
I bought three things — a notebook — two pens — and a folder.
I bought three things... a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
before.explanation: A comma after three things sets up the pause before the explanatory list.

after.prompt: Combine: I bought three things. They were a notebook, two pens, and a folder. Which version uses the pause before the list correctly?
choices: I bought three things: a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
I bought three things a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
I bought three things — a notebook — two pens — and a folder.
I bought three things... a notebook, two pens, and a folder.
after.explanation: A colon after three things sets up the list that follows.

before.prompt: Combine: The cat yowled at the door. The cat was enormous and grumpy. Which version uses strong parenthetical marks for the description?
choices: The cat — a enormous, grumpy tabby — yowled at the door.
The cat, a enormous, grumpy tabby, yowled at the door.
The cat... a enormous, grumpy tabby... yowled at the door.
The cat a enormous, grumpy tabby yowled at the door.
before.explanation: Dashes give the descriptive aside a sharp, emphatic interruption.

after.prompt: Combine: The cat yowled at the door. The cat was enormous and grumpy. Which version uses strong parenthetical marks for the description?
choices: The cat — an enormous, grumpy tabby — yowled at the door.
The cat, an enormous, grumpy tabby, yowled at the door.
The cat... an enormous, grumpy tabby... yowled at the door.
The cat an enormous, grumpy tabby yowled at the door.
after.explanation: Dashes give the descriptive aside a sharp, emphatic interruption.

before.prompt: A scientist caught an error in her published data. Which word best fits: She had to ______ the mistake publicly.
choices: admit
concede
acknowledge
confess
before.explanation: Confess implies guilt or wrongdoing, which is the connotation needed after being caught.

after.prompt: A scientist found an error in her published data. Which word best fits a neutral report: She had to ______ the mistake publicly.
choices: admit
concede
acknowledge
confess
after.explanation: Acknowledge means to state openly that something is true, the neutral word for correcting the record; confess implies guilt, and concede implies losing an argument.

before.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a colon to introduce a list of items?
choices: (1) The library contains; novels, biographies, and magazines.
(3) The library contains— novels: biographies and magazines.
(0) The library contains: novels, biographies, and magazines.
(2) The library contains novels, biographies, and magazines.
before.explanation: Option (0) correctly uses a colon to introduce the list 'novels, biographies, and magazines', making it the only sentence with proper colon usage.

after.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a colon to introduce a list of items?
choices: (1) The library contains; novels, biographies, and magazines.
(3) The library contains— novels: biographies and magazines.
The library contains the following: novels, biographies, and magazines.
(2) The library contains novels, biographies, and magazines.
after.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence, and 'The library contains the following' can stand alone.

before.prompt: Combine: (1) The janitor unlocked the doors at seven. (2) Students streamed into the gym. (3) The bell rang. Which combination avoids an inappropriate voice shift?
choices: The janitor unlocked the doors at seven, and students streamed into the gym before the bell rang.
The doors were unlocked at seven, and students streamed into the gym before the bell rang.
The janitor unlocked the doors at seven, and the gym was streamed into by students before the bell rang.
The doors were unlocked at seven, and the gym was streamed into by students before the bell rang.
before.explanation: Both clauses keep the passive voice with the doors and the gym as subjects, so no unmarked shift occurs.

after.prompt: Combine: (1) The janitor unlocked the doors at seven. (2) Students streamed into the gym. (3) The bell rang. Which combination avoids an inappropriate voice shift?
choices: The janitor unlocked the doors at seven, and students streamed into the gym before the bell rang.
The doors were unlocked at seven, and students streamed into the gym before the bell rang.
The janitor unlocked the doors at seven, and the gym was streamed into by students before the bell rang.
The doors were unlocked at seven, and the gym was streamed into by students before the bell rang.
after.explanation: Both clauses stay active, with the janitor and the students as the doers, so no unmarked shift occurs.

before.prompt: Combine: (1) The mayor proposed the budget. (2) The council rejected it. (3) She revised it. Which combination keeps a consistent passive voice?
choices: The mayor proposed the budget, and it was rejected by the council, and she revised it.
The budget was proposed by the mayor, and the council rejected it, and revisions were made by her.
The mayor proposed the budget, the council rejected it, and revisions were made by her.
The budget was proposed by the mayor, it was rejected by the council, and it was revised by her.
before.explanation: All three clauses stay passive with the actions done to the mayor and the budget, so the voice never shifts.

after.prompt: Combine: (1) The mayor proposed the budget. (2) The council rejected it. (3) She revised it. Which combination keeps a consistent passive voice?
choices: The mayor proposed the budget, and it was rejected by the council, and she revised it.
The budget was proposed by the mayor, and the council rejected it, and revisions were made by her.
The mayor proposed the budget, the council rejected it, and revisions were made by her.
The budget was proposed by the mayor, it was rejected by the council, and it was revised by her.
after.explanation: All three clauses stay passive, with the budget as the subject receiving each action, so the voice never shifts.

before.prompt: In dialogue, what does a dash at the end of a line usually show?
choices: shows a pause before an important word
shows an unfinished thought that trails off
shows a cut-off word in quoted speech
shows an interruption by another speaker
before.explanation: In dialogue, the dash shows that one speaker cuts another off mid-word.

after.prompt: In dialogue, what does a dash at the end of a line usually show?
choices: shows a pause before an important word
shows an unfinished thought that trails off
shows that a list is about to begin
shows an interruption by another speaker
after.explanation: In dialogue, a dash at the end of a line shows the speaker was cut off, usually by another speaker.

before.prompt: Which sentence best fits a model text that sets up a sharp, punchy explanation after a complete statement?
choices: She waited by the door — it never opened.
She waited by the door... it never opened.
She waited by the door, it never opened.
She waited by the door; it never opened.
before.explanation: A colon properly introduces the explanation that completes the first statement.

after.prompt: Which sentence best fits a model text that sets up a sharp, punchy explanation after a complete statement?
choices: She waited by the door — it never opened.
She waited by the door... it never opened.
She waited by the door, it never opened.
She waited by the door; it never opened.
after.explanation: A dash sets up a sharp, punchy payoff after a complete statement.

before.prompt: A writer wants a sentence to land on a surprise contrast: 'The team practiced daily, but lost.' How should the elements be arranged for the strongest effect?
choices: put the contrast clause first so readers expect a surprise
put the winning detail at the end so the sentence lands on it
make both halves exactly the same length
replace the contrast word with a neutral conjunction
before.explanation: Sentence-final position carries the most weight, so the winning detail belongs there.

after.prompt: A writer wants a sentence to land on a surprise contrast: 'The team practiced daily, but lost.' How should the elements be arranged for the strongest effect?
choices: put the contrast clause first so readers expect a surprise
put the loss at the end so the sentence lands on it
make both halves exactly the same length
replace the contrast word with a neutral conjunction
after.explanation: Sentence-final position carries the most weight, so the surprising loss belongs there.

before.prompt: Revise for clarity of causal relationship: 'Every branch is over twenty years old. The company is closing them.' Which revision best shows the second is a result of the first?
choices: Every branch is over twenty years old.
Because every branch is over twenty years old.
With every branch over twenty years old, being outdated.
Branches; every one over twenty years old.
before.explanation: Subordinating with Because makes clear that age is the cause, which the plain statement left ambiguous.

after.prompt: Revise for clarity of causal relationship: 'Every branch is over twenty years old. The company is closing them.' Which revision best shows the second is a result of the first?
choices: Every branch is over twenty years old.
Every branch is over twenty years old, so the company is closing them.
With every branch over twenty years old, being outdated.
Branches; every one over twenty years old.
after.explanation: So makes clear that the branches' age is the cause and the closing is the result.

before.prompt: The team won the championship, scoring twice in the last five minutes, stunning their rivals, delighting their fans. Fill in the blank: This is ______.

balanced, because the phrases mirror each other perfectly
cumulative, because the main idea opens and details trail after it
a fragment, because it lacks a finite verb
before.explanation: The main clause 'the crowd fell silent' comes first, and descriptive phrases are piled on after it — the classic cumulative shape.

after.prompt: The team won the championship, scoring twice in the last five minutes, stunning their rivals, delighting their fans. Fill in the blank: This is ______.
choices: periodic, because the main clause arrives at the very end
balanced, because the phrases mirror each other perfectly

a fragment, because it lacks a finite verb
after.explanation: The main clause 'The team won the championship' comes first, and descriptive phrases are piled on after it: the classic cumulative shape.

before.prompt: [Fill in the blank] Why is 'Because she was late' a fragment rather than a complete sentence? The best reason is ______.
choices: It is a fragment because it is too short.
It is a run-on because it has two clauses.
It is a balanced sentence because it mirrors ideas.
It is a fragment because it lacks a subject and a finite verb.
before.explanation: Shortness is not the problem; a fragment is missing a subject or a verb, so it cannot stand alone.

after.prompt: [Fill in the blank] Why is 'Because she was late' a fragment rather than a complete sentence? The best reason is ______.
choices: It is a fragment because it is too short.
It is a run-on because it has two clauses.
It is a balanced sentence because it mirrors ideas.
It is a fragment because 'Because' makes it a dependent clause that cannot stand alone.
after.explanation: Length is not the problem; it has a subject and a verb, but 'Because' leaves the thought unfinished.

before.prompt: Rewrite the sentence for suspense using a periodic structure: The lights suddenly went out.
choices: Out went the lights, and everyone fell silent.
Out the lights went suddenly, because everyone fell silent.
We suddenly went out the lights, and everyone fell silent.
The lights suddenly went out, and everyone fell silent.
before.explanation: “Out went the lights, and everyone fell silent” is correct because it uses periodic syntax by placing the prepositional phrase before the subject and verb, creating suspense.

after.prompt: Rewrite the sentence for suspense using a periodic structure: The lights suddenly went out.
choices: Suddenly, with everyone falling silent, out went the lights.
Out the lights went suddenly, because everyone fell silent.
We suddenly went out the lights, and everyone fell silent.
The lights suddenly went out, and everyone fell silent.
after.explanation: The main clause 'out went the lights' is held to the very end, which is what makes it periodic and builds suspense.

after.prompt: Which sentence is cumulative, meaning that it begins with the main clause and places additional details toward the end?

The children ran across the lawn, laughing and waving their colorful flags.
Across the lawn, laughing and waving their colorful flags, the children ran.

before.prompt: Why does 'She returned every borrowed book, even the one missing for a year' put more emphasis on the missing book than 'Even the one missing for a year, she returned every borrowed book'?

It puts the newest information at the start of the sentence.
It ends on the borrowed books, the point the reader is meant to notice last.
It makes the sentence longer, and length always adds emphasis.
before.explanation: End position is the strongest spot in a sentence, so the material placed last gets the emphasis.

after.prompt: Why does 'She returned every borrowed book, even the one missing for a year' put more emphasis on the missing book than 'Even the one missing for a year, she returned every borrowed book'?
choices: It repeats the word library twice, which adds rhythm.

after.prompt: What fault does 'The bell rang the students bolted' commit when two sentences are merged without punctuation?

It turns two complete sentences into one unpunctuated run-on.

after.explanation: Joining two independent clauses with nothing between them creates a fused sentence, a kind of run-on.
